Microchannel TES results and discussion The microchannel design offers several advantages over the original round-tube design, including a lower fluid inventory, a larger internal tube surface area (2.9x higher), and lower resistances between the fluid streams (channels are in direct contact) and between the channel walls and composite PCM (3x reduction in the contact resistance). However, the surface area between the channel walls and composite PCM is lower in the microchannel design (6.45 m2 vs 8.26 m2) because only half of the flat channel is in contact with the storage medium. The reduced surface area is partially mitigated by the ability for heat to spread through the finned microchannel structures. The performance of the microchannel heat exchanger design was quantified for 36 different hybrid charge/discharge rates. An example case is described below, with a charge rate from the refrigerant of about 11.8 kW (3.4 tons) and a discharge rate from the glycol of about 3.5 kW (1.0 ton). The SOC throughout the charging process is similar for the two designs, as shown in Figure 14. This is expected because the capacity and net heat transfer rate from the composite PCM are nearly identical in the two components. The only differences arise in the amount of thermal storage outside of the composite PCM. The serpentine round-tube design has a larger fluid inventory that requires more thermal energy to heat it up. The larger amount of thermal storage in the fluid results in slightly longer charging times. Although the SOC is similar between the two designs, the change in the PCM state is accomplished at different fluid temperatures. The glycol outlet and refrigerant temperatures during the charging process are shown in Figure 15. The lower resistances in the microchannel design result in lower refrigerant temperatures and higher glycol outlet temperatures. The improved performance has system-level benefits because the compressor operates more efficiently. The system results are discussed more in Section 7.
